_why: The DECLARED INTENT for the Vercel WAF rules on project `sairn`, kept in git
because the live config is not. A firewall rule lives in Vercel's dashboard,
so it is invisible to git log, to every reviewer, and to every gate in this
repository -- somebody can disable it and nothing here would ever say so.
That is not hypothetical. api/_lib/anon-rate-limit.js shipped ENFORCING and
was measured completely inert in production: 40 concurrent junk-token
requests returned 40 x 401 and not one 429. A protection nobody verifies is
not a protection, and the same failure one layer up is a rule somebody
switched off in March that nobody notices until it is needed.
tools/waf_rule_check.py compares the LIVE config against this file. Change
this file in the same commit as the rule, never afterwards -- a spec edited
to match reality is a spec that has stopped checking anything.

rules.name: anon-api-observe-100
rules._purpose: Observation threshold 1 of 2. Logs, never blocks. Set deliberately LOW -- a ten-workstation practice syncing 16 resources can plausibly cross it -- because the question this week answers is 'how often would a plausible enforce ceiling have fired, and on whom'. A threshold nothing ever crosses teaches nothing.

rules.name: anon-api-observe-600
rules._purpose: Observation threshold 2 of 2, so the week yields a DISTRIBUTION rather than one bit. 600/60s is well above any plausible legitimate burst, so anything crossing it is worth looking at directly.

_invariant_that_outlives_these_two_rules: EVERY rule listed here must have rate_limit.action == 'log' until the
open-work row for the anon amplification says otherwise IN WRITING.
The checker enforces that separately from the per-rule comparison, so
flipping a rule to block by editing this file still trips a distinct,
loud failure rather than sliding through as a spec update.
